status: Phase B. Pre/post items are parallel forms aligned to objectives 1-5 (design/alignment-matrix.md). Facts cite research/sources.md rows. Transfer items use a CONSTRUCTED scenario, labelled as such.

pre.prompt: A glacier's terminus stays in the same place for ten years. What is the ice doing?

options.text: The ice has stopped moving
options.why: No. Ice can keep flowing downhill while the terminus holds still, because melting at the end balances the supply (NPS).

options.text: Ice keeps flowing downhill, and melting or calving at the end balances the supply
options.why: Yes. NPS: the glacier can stop advancing 'though the body of ice is still moving down the mountain'.

options.text: The glacier is growing thicker every year
options.why: Not necessarily. A steady terminus says nothing on its own about thickness.

pre.prompt: Which of these can a pair of photos from the same viewpoint show directly?

options.text: That ice and vegetation changed between the two dates
options.why: Yes. Repeat photos show visible change at the same place.

options.text: The cause of the change
options.why: No. Photos show what changed, not why.

options.text: The exact year the ice left each spot
options.why: No. Two photos only bracket the change between their dates.

pre.prompt: A source says a glacier retreated 'more than 3 km' in 9 years. What can you say about its average rate?

options.text: Exactly 0.33 km per year
options.why: No. 'More than' makes 3 km a minimum, so 0.33 km/yr is a minimum too.

options.text: At least about 0.33 km per year
options.why: Yes. 3 / 9 is about 0.33, and the true average is at least that.

options.text: At most 0.33 km per year
options.why: No. That reverses the bound.

pre.prompt: Muir Glacier had been retreating since about the mid-1700s. What does this suggest?

options.text: Recent climate change cannot be involved
options.why: No. A long retreat does not rule out later causes; it means more than one factor may be at work.

options.text: The retreat seen after 1941 may have more than one cause
options.why: Yes. NPS: advance or retreat reflects snowfall, topography and climate trends, and tidewater glaciers are more complicated.

options.text: The photos must be wrong
options.why: No. The long history and the photos are consistent.

pre.prompt: Bare rock is exposed by a retreating glacier. What usually comes first?

options.text: Spruce and hemlock forest
options.why: No. NPS describes mature spruce-hemlock forest as the late stage.

options.text: Moss and other small pioneer plants
options.why: Yes. NPS: moss colonizes glacial till, paving the way for plants that follow.

options.text: Nothing can ever grow on glacial ground
options.why: No. Glacier Bay is a classic site of plant succession.

post.prompt: Why can a glacier's terminus retreat even while its ice keeps flowing forward?

options.text: Because melting and calving at the end remove ice faster than flow brings it
options.why: Yes. Retreat means loss at the terminus outpaces supply (NPS).

options.text: Because the ice flows uphill
options.why: No. Glacier ice flows downhill.

options.text: Because the bedrock moves
options.why: No. The bedrock is not what moves the terminus.

post.prompt: In the 2004 photo, what does the trimline on the far slope tell you?

options.text: Roughly how thick the ice was in 1941
options.why: Yes. USGS: the 1941 ice thickness correlates with the trimline.

options.text: Where the sea level was in 1941
options.why: No. The trimline marks the old ice surface, not sea level.

options.text: Where a forest fire stopped
options.why: No. Nothing in the record suggests fire.

post.prompt: 1941 to 2004: more than 7 km in 63 years. Which statement is best?

options.text: The glacier retreated 0.11 km every single year
options.why: No. That is an average, and a minimum. The 1941-1950 average was at least 0.33 km/yr, so the rate was not constant.

options.text: The average was at least about 0.11 km/yr, and the rate changed over time
options.why: Yes. A lower-bound average, and the faster 1941-1950 minimum shows it varied.

options.text: The glacier must have advanced between 1950 and 2004
options.why: Not supported. The sources do not say that; they only give minimum totals.

post.prompt: Which is the most careful explanation of Muir Glacier's retreat?

options.text: It is caused only by recent warming
options.why: Too strong. Retreat began about 1750, and tidewater dynamics matter too.

options.text: It has nothing to do with climate
options.why: Too strong. NPS lists climate trends among the factors.

options.text: Several factors (climate, snowfall, topography, tidewater calving) likely combine; the photos alone cannot split them
options.why: Yes. That matches the evidence and states its limits.

post.prompt: Ground near the 2004 viewpoint has shrubs. If nothing disturbs it, what does the NPS sequence suggest comes later?

options.text: Back to bare rock
options.why: No. The sequence moves toward forest, not back to rock.

options.text: Spruce growing up under alder, then spruce-hemlock forest
options.why: Yes, though the sources give no timing for Muir Inlet.

options.text: Moss replacing the shrubs
options.why: No. Moss is an early stage.

transfer.label: Constructed for teaching purposes. 'Glacier X' is fictional; the numbers are invented to practise the method and are not data about any real glacier.
transfer.scenario: Two photos of fictional Glacier X are taken from the same rock outcrop, 20 years apart. A survey note says the terminus retreated 'at least 1.2 km' in that time. In the later photo, moss and small plants grow on the newly exposed ground near the outcrop.

items.prompt: What is the lowest average retreat rate consistent with the note?

options.text: 0.06 km/yr (a minimum)
options.why: Yes. 1.2 / 20 = 0.06, and 'at least' makes it a lower bound.

options.text: 0.6 km/yr
options.why: No. Check the division: 1.2 / 20 = 0.06.

options.text: Exactly 0.06 km/yr
options.why: Close, but 'at least' means it is a minimum, not an exact value.

items.prompt: Glacier X ends in the sea. A classmate says 'This proves the local climate warmed.' What is the best reply?

options.text: Agree: retreat always means warming
options.why: Too strong. Tidewater glaciers can retreat through calving dynamics too.

options.text: It is consistent with warming, but we would need climate records and data on calving and fjord depth to say how much each factor matters
options.why: Yes. Names the evidence needed.

options.text: Photos can never tell us anything
options.why: No. They show what changed; they just cannot show why on their own.

items.prompt: Predict the ground near the outcrop in another few decades, if undisturbed.

options.text: Plants that enrich the soil (such as Dryas or alder), then shrubs and eventually trees
options.why: Yes, if Glacier X follows a sequence like the one NPS describes at Glacier Bay. That is an assumption to state.

options.text: Instant forest
options.why: No. Succession takes stages.

options.text: Always bare
options.why: No. Moss is already growing.
